# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles spatial coordinates and multi-period population series for 1.169 individually assessed settlements across ancient and mediaeval Sudan and Nubia between 2500BC and 1821AD (940 in Sudan, 95 in South Sudan, 31 in Ethiopia and 49 in Eritrea). Screened from 1.177 candidate towns, archaeological tells, royal cemeteries, river forts and caravan depots (8 duplicate aliases merged), the retained sites span eight ecological and political sub-regions from Lower Nubia and the Dongola Reach through Butana, the Beja Red Sea coast, the Funj Gezira, Darfur, Kordofan and the Shilluk-Upper Nile wetlands. Active assessed centres expand from 90 at 2000BC to 180 at year 0, 283 at 500AD, 577 at 1000AD, 688 at 1500AD and 51 at 1820AD, tracing urban leadership from Kerma (14,7k) and Napata (16,4k) to Meroe (29,4k), Old Dongola (23,8k), Soba (32,4k) and Sennar (28,6k).



# Background

Reconstructing urban settlement across ancient and mediaeval Sudan requires integrating rescue archaeology from the Nile cataracts with mediaeval Arabic chronicles, early modern travel narratives and regional historical syntheses [@Adams1977Nubia; @Edwards2004NubianPast; @Pleiades2024Africa]. Unlike densely surveyed river plains in Egypt or Mesopotamia, Sudanese settlements divide sharply between fortified mudbrick river towns along the Nile cataracts, rain-fed *hafir* complexes across the Butana steppe, Red Sea coral ports and dispersed upland or caravan towns in Darfur and Kordofan [@Bobrowski2023Ltd1Kerma; @Costanzo2021CreatingThe; @Spaulding1985HeroicAge]. Uniting these trajectories in one coordinate-anchored ledger tracks the four-millennium southward migration of Sudan's urban core.

# Methodology

## Screening, Sub-Regional Assignment and Benchmarks

Candidate settlements were compiled from excavation reports, surface surveys, Pleiades coordinates [@Pleiades2024Africa] and historical monographs [@Adams1977Nubia; @Edwards2004NubianPast; @Spaulding1985HeroicAge]. Eight duplicate spelling aliases were merged into canonical records, leaving 1.169 unique settlements (5.725 dated observations), all recorded on a city-proper basis. Each settlement is assigned to one of the eight vector sub-regions defined for the chapter domain (with the four sites sitting immediately outside the five-arcminute interior mask grouped into their nearest contiguous hydrological corridor). Tables 1 to 8 present linearly interpolated resident populations at six benchmarks (2000BC, year 0, 500AD, 1000AD, 1500AD and 1820AD) alongside each site's peak population and peak date, marking pre-foundation or post-abandonment intervals with a hyphen (-).

# Testing and Validation

Across the 131 spatially deduplicated centres (merging overlapping Wad Medani coordinates), peak populations follow a sub-unitary Pareto rank-size slope of $q = 0,74$ ($R^2 = 0,98$) over the leading 66 settlements and $q = 1,03$ ($R^2 = 0,79$) across the full ledger (Figure \ref{fig:settlements-rank}). All 1.169 sites match modern national boundaries [@Runfola2020GeoBoundaries] and align chronologically with their documented foundation and abandonment horizons [@Budka2023DayThe; @Nasreldein2026ContinuityChange].

# Results

# Limitations

Three caveats govern use of this settlement ledger. First, northern cataract towns salvaged prior to reservoir inundation benefit from far denser excavation coverage than western or southern Sudanese savanna towns [@Naser2019DialoguesThe; @Bashir2026ArchaeologyAnd]. Second, urban estimates derived from walled footprints or eighteenth-century traveller house counts carry roughly 15% to 25% uncertainty [@Budka2023DayThe]. Third, the 1.169 retained centres represent the nucleated urban and royal tier and should be read alongside the kriged rural population totals in the companion review.

# Conclusion

Together, the 1.169 settlements trace four millennia of urban transformation from Kerma and Napata to Meroe, Old Dongola, Soba, Suakin, Sennar, El Fasher and Kodok, documenting Sudan's long shift from northern riverine cataracts to the rain-fed savanna interior by 1821AD.
